longForm.title: The Battle of Pavia, 1525: How a King Rode His Cavalry Into an Arquebus Ambush and Lost an Era
longForm.excerpt: On February 24, 1525, Francis I of France charged his gendarmerie into prepared arquebusier positions, lost his army, his freedom, and France's dominance in Italy — and showed Europe what the next century of warfare would look like.
paragraphs: On the morning of February 24, 1525, King Francis I of France occupied a position that looked, by the conventional military arithmetic of his time, reasonably strong. His army of approximately 28,000 men had been besieging the Imperial-held city of Pavia for three months. The garrison was running short of supplies. The relief force — roughly 23,000 men under the Viceroy of Naples, Charles de Lannoy, and the Marquis of Pescara, Fernando de Ávalos — had arrived too late to prevent the encirclement and was numerically inferior to the French. Several of Francis's senior commanders urged withdrawal: maintain the siege, let the city starve, and deny the Imperials the engagement they needed. Francis chose to fight. The 25th birthday of his rival, Emperor Charles V, fell on that date, though historians are divided on whether this influenced the decision or whether it was simply an artifact of memoir-writing. What the sources agree on is that Francis ordered his cavalry to attack before his Swiss infantry was in position to support the charge, and that the consequences were immediate and catastrophic.

The instrument of his destruction was the Spanish tercio. The tercios were the organizational innovation of the Italian Wars — integrated formations combining Swiss-style pikemen with arquebusiers in proportions that had been refined through a generation of fighting on Italian soil. The Marquis of Pescara had approximately 3,000 arquebusiers distributed through his infantry formations at Pavia, pre-positioned in the hedgerows and tree lines of the Mirabello deer park where the battle would be fought. The arquebus of 1525 was not a rapid-fire weapon; it took a trained soldier roughly 30 seconds to reload. But against cavalry committed to a charge across open ground with no room to maneuver, 30 seconds was irrelevant. What mattered was range, and the arquebusiers at Pavia were able to engage the French gendarmerie at ranges that made the charge suicidal before the cavalry could close to fighting distance.

Francis made his error in the opening minutes. His plan required his Swiss pike blocks — the core of the French infantry, Swiss mercenaries who had dominated European land warfare for fifty years — to advance in coordination with his cavalry to prevent exactly the kind of enfilading fire that Pescara had prepared. Instead, when the Imperial forces broke through the park wall before dawn and advanced through the morning mist, Francis ordered his cavalry to attack immediately. He then positioned himself at the head of his mounted force, between the cavalry and the Swiss, which meant the pikemen could not advance without riding through him. The Swiss halted. The gendarmerie charged. The arquebusiers opened fire.

Contemporary accounts — from the Spanish captain Francisco de Salazar, from the French chronicler Martin du Bellay, from the letters of Lannoy to Charles V written the same day — agree on the speed of what followed. The French heavy cavalry, the finest mounted arm in Europe, was effectively destroyed in a quarter-hour. Richard de la Pole, the Yorkist claimant to the English throne and one of the most experienced cavalry commanders in French service, was killed in the first phase of the action. Anne de Montmorency's company broke. The French artillery, which represented a genuine advantage — Francis had invested heavily in his train and his gunners were among the best in Europe — was rendered useless when the cavalry retreated back through it. The gunners had been overrun before they could reposition. By the time the Swiss entered the fighting, they were engaging Imperial infantry that had already defeated the French cavalry and reorganized.

Francis I fought personally throughout the battle, which was in keeping with his self-conception as a chivalric sovereign but which placed the most valuable prisoner in Europe in unnecessary danger. His horse was killed under him. He fought on foot. When his attendants saw that the battle was irretrievably lost, they supported him against a wall and held the press of bodies until Imperial soldiers arrived to take him. The men who captured the King of France included Wilhelm von Baumgartner, a Flemish captain of the Imperial household infantry. By midmorning on February 24, Francis was a prisoner. The Duke of Suffolk, Louis de la Trémoille, and Galiot de Genouillac — among the senior French commanders — were killed in the action. French casualties are estimated at 8,000 to 10,000 dead, with a similar number captured. Imperial losses were perhaps 700 to 1,000.

The news reached Paris before the end of February. Francis's mother, Louise of Savoy, serving as regent in her son's absence, received a letter whose most famous line has been reduced in popular memory to a single phrase: 'All is lost except honor.' The actual French text — 'tout est perdu fors l'honneur et la vie' — translates as 'all is lost except honor and life,' which is somewhat less dramatic and somewhat more informative about Francis's state of mind. He was asking his mother to manage the political consequences, and she did: keeping the kingdom intact in the absence of the king, beginning the diplomatic maneuvering that would eventually secure his release, and making the preliminary approaches to the Ottoman Sultan Suleiman I that would inaugurate the Franco-Ottoman alliance — a Catholic monarchy in formal cooperation with the Islamic world against the Holy Roman Emperor, one of the more remarkable diplomatic relationships of the century.

The Treaty of Madrid, signed January 14, 1526, required Francis to surrender Burgundy — the territorial prize Charles had wanted since the death of his grandmother Mary — along with all French claims in Italy, Flanders, and Artois. Francis signed, having previously arranged for a legal protest to be registered nullifying his consent on grounds of duress. He also sent his two sons, the Dauphin Francis and Henry Duke of Orléans, to Spain as hostages against his compliance with the treaty. He was released in March 1526. By May 1526 he had repudiated the treaty, formed the League of Cognac with Pope Clement VII, Venice, Florence, and Francesco Sforza, and was at war with the Empire again. His sons remained in Spanish custody for four years, in conditions that deteriorated significantly after their father's repudiation. Whether Francis's conduct should be read as political necessity — a treaty signed under duress is not binding under the law of nations as it was then understood — or as a straightforward failure of personal integrity is a question that French and Spanish historians have not yet settled to mutual satisfaction.

The battle's military significance outlasted its diplomatic consequences. Pavia demonstrated, with a clarity that the Italian Wars had been building toward for thirty years, what arquebusiers in integrated formation could do to the finest heavy cavalry in Europe when the cavalry was committed without infantry support and had no room to maneuver. The Swiss pike block was not made obsolete by a single afternoon — it remained a central element of European armies for another generation — but its assumed invulnerability was broken. The tercio system that Pescara and his predecessors had developed in the Italian Wars, integrating fire and pike in mutually supporting formations, became the dominant infantry model in Europe for the next century. Spanish hegemony in Italy was settled at Pavia and not seriously challenged again until the French entered Italy under Louis XIV, 140 years later.

What Pavia did not settle was the broader competition between France and the Habsburgs. Francis understood, eventually, that he could not defeat Spain in Italy by conventional means and win. Charles understood that he could not eliminate France as a strategic problem — a France at peace in the west would find allies in the east, and the Franco-Ottoman alliance that Louise of Savoy had begun to assemble during her son's captivity was already taking shape. The Italian Wars continued for another thirty years after Pavia, through the reigns of Henry II and Philip II of Spain, until the Treaty of Cateau-Cambrésis in 1559 finally settled the question of Italian dominion in Spain's favor. Pavia changed who held the advantage in that contest. It did not end the contest.

shortForm.title: The USS Pueblo Incident, 1968: The Cold War's Most Peculiar Capture
shortForm.excerpt: On January 23, 1968, North Korea seized the USS Pueblo in international waters. The crew spent eleven months in captivity. The ship never came back. The intelligence loss was among the most damaging of the Cold War.
paragraphs: On January 23, 1968, the USS Pueblo (AGER-2), a United States Navy signals intelligence vessel operating approximately 15 nautical miles off the coast of North Korea near Wonsan, was boarded and seized by North Korean naval forces. Commander Lloyd Bucher and 82 crew members became prisoners of the government of Kim Il-sung. The Pueblo was the first US Navy vessel seized by a foreign power in peacetime since 1807, when HMS Leopard fired on USS Chesapeake and impressed members of her crew into the Royal Navy — a comparison that tells you something about how the Johnson administration experienced the next eleven months.

The Pueblo had been on station for three days when North Korean patrol boats ordered it to heave to. Bucher's standing orders were ambiguous on what to do in exactly this scenario. He maneuvered to avoid contact. A North Korean subchaser fired warning shots, then fired for effect, striking the vessel and wounding crew members. Bucher transmitted a report and an emergency destruction order; the crew was given approximately twelve minutes to destroy classified material before the North Koreans were aboard. Much of it was not destroyed. The intelligence loss — signals collection equipment, KW-7 cipher machine contact cards, codebooks, and cryptographic keying material — was assessed by the National Security Agency as among the most serious single intelligence compromises of the Cold War. Soviet intelligence, which received the captured material from Pyongyang, was subsequently able to read encrypted US Navy communications for a period that NSA later estimated at years.

The crew spent eleven months in North Korean custody, during which they were subjected to systematic beatings, staged interrogations, and what the surviving crew members described as a sustained effort to extract signed confessions to espionage in North Korean territorial waters. Bucher eventually signed a confession after, he testified later, his captors threatened to execute crew members one by one in front of him if he refused. The crew was released December 23, 1968, after the United States signed a document admitting to espionage — a document the US simultaneously repudiated at the moment of signing, having informed the North Koreans in advance that it would do so. One crew member, Duane Hodges, had been killed in the capture. The USS Pueblo was never returned and is displayed in Pyongyang on the Pothong River as a museum ship, the only commissioned vessel of the United States Navy currently in the possession of a foreign government.

onThisDay.headline: Dos de Mayo: Madrid Rises Against French Occupation
onThisDay.summary: On May 2, 1808, Spanish civilians and soldiers in Madrid rose against French forces occupying the city under Marshal Joachim Murat, in what became known as the Dos de Mayo Uprising. The revolt was triggered by the forced removal of the Spanish royal family to France; French cavalry and infantry suppressed the fighting by evening, followed by mass executions of captives the following morning — the scene immortalized by Francisco Goya in 'The Third of May 1808.' The uprising is considered the opening act of the Peninsular War, the six-year conflict that tied down 300,000 French troops and which Napoleon later called 'the Spanish ulcer.'
